abstract: A functional definition of a membrane protein's structure is the three-dimensional arrangement of the polypeptide and the structure of the membrane around it. Biological membranes are composed of self-assembled lipid bilayers, with membrane proteins acting as inclusions that perturb this phase. These inclusions induce long-range changes in membrane structure and create an intrinsic, lipid-mediated driving force for membrane protein association. The question is how much different membrane protein folds shape their surrounding membrane to tune the affinity and specificity of this driving force. To investigate this, we conducted a computational study to evaluate whether different membrane protein oligomers exhibit characteristic membrane defects that indicate specificity in complexation. We performed coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of monomeric and oligomeric states of ten different channels and transporters in POPC bilayers and evaluated changes in membrane thickness, deformation energy, and lipid packing parameters. We found that all the proteins affect their surrounding membrane up to 3 nm from the protein surface. However, we observed larger defects at oligomeric interfaces for obligatory or structurally monomorphic complexes, suggesting that their oligomerization is partly driven by burial of membrane defects. In contrast, oligomers that adopt different quaternary structures across homologs show weaker perturbations at known binding interfaces, and larger perturbations at lipid-facing surfaces. Nevertheless, all systems show fewer membrane defects upon oligomerization, suggesting an underlying lipid-mediated driving force that each protein fold modulates to tune affinity via membrane-mediated oligomerization.
